newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghanistan rules out compromise over Islam.
newsitem.headline: Afghanistan rules out compromise over Islam.

text.p: Afghanistan's new Taleban rulers rejected U.N. and international concern over its restrictions on women's rights, saying that while it would make changes, it would not compromise the Islamic pillars of its policies.

But U.N. and other aid groups said after a meeting with acting foreign minister Mullah Mohammed Ghous they were optimistic a compromise could be reached that would let them resume operations employing and supporting women in the country.

"The changes may occur in some other spheres; like we will evacuate our people who are in the city at the moment and of course we will bring more regularities to the government, but Islam does not accept change," acting information minister Amir Khan Mutaqi told a news conference.
"For the last 1,400 years no change has occured in Islam," he said. "These principles are eternal and will remain eternal."

In separate statements on Monday, the United Nations and United States expressed concern about the Taleban's decrees restricting women's activities, saying such limitations may jeopardise aid and finance projects and could isolate Kabul's new government.
The cautiously worded statements were the first expressions of concern by Washington or the world body, but human rights groups and neighbours opposing the Taleban have criticised its government.

Representatives of the United Nations and non-governmental groups, whose operations have largely ground to a halt since the Taleban takeover on September 27, said they had expressed concern and called for a return to the status quo of 11 days ago.

"We're certainly trying to avoid a collision course... We believe there will be some room for manoeuvre after continual dialogue between us and I think we have opened up the dialogue today," said Charles MacFadden, executive director of the Agency Coordinating Body for Afghan Relief (ACBAR).
Aid workers said the Taleban had been astonished by the reaction of the international community to its takeover and implementation of strict Sharia, or Islamic law.

Thousands of educated Afghans have fled the capital saying they cannot live under strict rules that require most women to stay home, most girls to forego education and men to grow beards and attend prayers five times a day.

"We pointed out to the foreign minister there is not enough security if people do not have sufficient food. Ghous said, 'wait slowly, it will be done', but the agencies' common point was that there is not enough time and we are running out of it," Thierry Pitzner, head of the Kabul office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, told reporters.
MacFadden and Pitzner said they had requested another meeting on Tuesday and a ruling on policy by the Taleban within two weeks.
"We hope that with a little bit of pragmatism they will be able to adjust to a position which can enable us fully with our activities," MacFadden said.

The Taleban's Mutaqi said his government felt it was unfair that despite bringing peace and security to much of the country, Kabul's new rulers were being deprived of recognition by the international community.

"Although a big change has happened in Afghanistan which has happened with the help and in accordance with the wishes of the people, still the international community has not recognised our government," he said.
